In 2005, a few college buddies and I traveled to Oventik, one of the Zapatista Caracoles. It was an adventure that almost got us killed several times, due to a few factors: the road to get there (up in the mountains and a lot of turns, next to cliffs), and the fact that the car we rented was on its last legs.

Also, upon arriving to San Cristobal de las Casas we spoke to the only white man there, who sat us down at a cafe (he appeared to be from the CIA) and asked us straight up, “Why are you here, who are you with and what do you plan on doing and when are you leaving?”

For about 5 minutes we felt important enough for the empire to actually give a shit about us. 😂

In 2005, a few college friends and I visited Oventik, one of the Zapatista caracoles in Chiapas. We nearly died several times getting there. The mountain road wrapped around cliffs, and our rental car was barely functioning—a nice combination when you’re trying to visit a revolution.

In San Cristóbal de las Casas, the only white man we met sat us down in a café and questioned us so directly that he appeared to be a CIA agent. Why were we there? Who did we work with? What were our plans? When were we leaving?

community-s9a.u2-emuA:
One feature I like in particular is the idea of “mandar obedeciendo” – leaders, or rather representatives, are mandated to obey the decisions of the assemblies.

And the Zapatistas are the closest I’ve come to seeing this in its entirety. It’s not just a way of making decisions, but an entire way of running aspects of life like education, health, justice, collective production, political formation, and teaching others, to name a few, all coordinated on a larger scale.
community-s9a.u2-emuB:
It’s not just the “mandar obedeciendo” (leading by obeying) model of representation, where political representatives are representatives in that they represent what the assemblies have decided and have to answer to the assemblies.

It’s the Zapatistas that come closest in toto to what I’m looking for, I think. Not just in the way they vote but also in how they organise their education, their healthcare, their justice system, their production (mostly collective), their political formation, their formation of other people, and how these are coordinated beyond the village level.
community-s9a.u2:
What impressed me most was their form of authority: mandar obedeciendo, leading by obeying. Representatives carry assembly decisions and remain answerable to the people who gave the mandate.

The Zapatistas are also the closest whole example I found because autonomy there is not merely a voting method. They have built their own education, health, justice, collective production, political formation, and ways of teaching outsiders, while coordinating beyond a single village.
community-s9a.u3-emuA:
In 2023, the Zapatistas made a major change to their organizational structure. They dissolved their Municipalities (MZR’s) and Good Government Juntas after an extensive internal review. Now, each community has a Local Autonomous Government, which may or may not choose to link up with other communities in a regional collective. But no matter what, the coordination levels are not above the local levels; they’re below.

Institutions generally become more layered over time. The Zapatistas reviewed their institutions and went in the opposite direction. Imagine if, after a hundred year review, the US government decided the best solution was to dissolve itself and give all authority back to local governments. Of course, that will never happen because it would require leaders to give up power. The Zapatistas didn’t write a book on how to be a good leader and then start a program to certify people as good leaders. They changed the system they were living in.
community-s9a.u3-emuB:
In a recent communique (2023), the zapatistas explained that, after a long review process, they were dissolving their Municipalities (MAREZ) and Good Government Juntas, and transferring power to the Local Autonomous Government of each community, with the possibility to form regional collectives for coordination. It is clear in the text that these coordinating levels are not above the local ones, but below, subordinate to each community.

While most institutions tend to become more layered as time goes by, the zapatistas have taken the time to review their process and move power even lower. Not by creating a book on leadership and starting a certification program, but by actually changing the system they are living in.
community-s9a.u3:
In 2023, the Zapatistas announced that they were dissolving the Rebel Zapatista Autonomous Municipalities and Good Government Juntas after a long internal review. Their new arrangement moved authority toward Local Autonomous Governments in each community. Those local bodies can coordinate through regional collectives, but the coordinating levels are explicitly described as dependent on the communities rather than superior to them.

Most institutions accumulate layers and offices as they age. The Zapatistas reviewed theirs and pushed authority downward. They did not issue a leadership book and open a certification program. They changed the system they were actually living in.
community-s9a.u4-emuA:
Also I have to restrain my enthusiasm for the model, because in a new ecovillage, where the people are without the long history of struggle and connection (like land, language, etc…) that the indigenous zapatistas have, it would be hard to implement this kind of structure directly.

The zapatistas say that there is nothing to import or export from zapatismo, but I think that the key of their diagram is the ability to change it, based on experience. They built something, then they learned something, then they changed the structure of what they…
community-s9a.u4-emuB:
Here is where I have to rein myself in a bit, as I know that the Zapatistas are in a position that most new ecovillages are not, because they are coming from communities with a history, struggles over the same land, a common language, often a common kinship, and often decades of common defense. So it wouldn’t work for a new ecovillage to just draw the above diagram and expect everything to work out.

In fact, the Zapatistas say repeatedly that one cannot import or export Zapatismo. The idea, rather, is to learn from them. In this case, the idea is to build something, and then be willing to change it when one finds that it doesn’t work.
community-s9a.u4:
This is also where I need to restrain my enthusiasm. Zapatista autonomy grew from Indigenous communities with long histories, shared land struggles, language, kinship, and decades of collective defense. A new ecovillage cannot copy the visible diagram and instantly acquire the trust beneath it.

The Zapatistas themselves have warned people not to import or export Zapatismo as a ready-made model. The useful thing is not their diagram. It is how they learn: build, ask, discover where practice fails, and change the structure.
community-s9a.u5-emuA: Those don't actually show their entire economic path to getting where they are, starting with internal necessities that are unpriced, to a common purse and out with the rest of the money. They certainly show that there are many things that can be done collectively, from supporting schools and clinics to funding their own government and resistance. They still sell things, trade, and need outside support. And those are, I think, good points about the dangers of relying on outside support.
community-s9a.u5-emuB: Also this isn't proof that I'm against a total path away from the use of money, just to clarify. My point is just that even going from nothing to taking some internal necessities off of the market and pooling the work for a common purpose (which is what the Zapatistas have done to provide for schools, medical care, government, and the means of resistance) is a great advancement, even if they need to make money by selling products and even rely on some help from outside sources (which can be a bit of a trap if not managed well).
community-s9a.u5: They are also not proof of my complete economic path from unpriced internal necessities, to a common purse, to eliminating outside money. Zapatista communities use collective work to support schools, clinics, autonomous government, and resistance; they also sell products, trade, and receive outside support. What they demonstrate is that major necessities and public functions can be taken out of ordinary market purchase and governed collectively. Outside help can build capability, but it can also create gatekeepers and uneven dependence when the specialist, donor, or organization remains indispensable.
community-s9a.u6-emuA:
In celebration of ten years of building autonomous governments, the Zapatistas organized an Escuelita where those from outside their territories could come and stay with families and learn how they do it. There were about 1,500 students at the first ones and there have been thousands at subsequent ones.

There are ways of running an escuelita that screw up the communities that host it and see it as a business. In that case, like when it’s run as a resort, the people who live there have to live for outsiders and the number of guests become the measurement of success, instead of how many daughter communities are being created. It’s not about changing the people who visit, but about teaching them the social and material system well enough that they can implement it elsewhere.
community-s9a.u6-emuB:
As part of the 10 anniversary of their autonomous government, the Zapatistas opened an Escuelita where non-Zappestas could stay with families and learn about how their autonomy works in practice. The first Escuelitas had about 1500 students and the subsequent ones had even more in the thousands.

One way the escuelita’s could have failed is if the peoples who run them had turned it into a business and made it so that all their life was oriented towards impressing outsiders who paid to stay with them. Then the measure of success would be how many people come stay with them rather than how many daughter communities are created. Their goal is not to simply transform people (though that may happen) but to show people how their social and material system works so that others can learn from it and create something else from it.
community-s9a.u6:
For the tenth anniversary of their autonomous governments, the Zapatistas opened the Escuelita. Outsiders lived with families and learned autonomy by participating in ordinary life. The first sessions brought around 1,500 students, with later sessions bringing thousands more.

An escuelita can fail by becoming a visitor business. Residents spend their lives performing community for paying outsiders, and guest numbers replace daughter communities as the success metric. The point is not to make people feel transformed for a week. It is to teach enough of the social and material system that some can build elsewhere.
community-s9a.u7-emuA:
One of the things I looked into while doing research for this post was whether or not there was any follow up to the Escuelita. There are, of course, alumni, and people who took what they learned with them when they went home, and have been working to organize in various ways since, but it’s hard to find examples of people who took what they learned at the Escuelita and then went on to create new institutions, and then even harder to find out how those institutions are doing now. Plus, of course, the Zapatistas have been influential in other spaces internationally well before the Escuelita. But I don’t feel like this in any way detracts from what I’m trying to do here, which is, to borrow a pedagogy, and take on the ambition of trying to replicate it.

Also, I should note here, that many of these forms have been explored in the context of Sociocracy .
community-s9a.u7-emuB:
I have tried to find this as well in my research, but was unable to find much. Yes, there are networks of those who attended the Escuelita and many tried to take what they learned and implement it in their own countries, but I have been unable to find direct links between this and specific institutions that were subsequently created or studies on the effects of these institutions on those who have participated in them and their kids. The other thing to consider is that the Zapatistas were already influencing people internationally before the Escuelita started, so it is hard to say if any subsequent institutions were influenced by it or not. For me, I don't even think this is really necessary. I don't need them to have done it successfully already in order for me to try to replicate their pedagogy.

Sociocracy has some similar forms, but a completely different history.
community-s9a.u7:
In my research, I also tried to trace what happened after the Escuelita. I found alumni networks, people carrying practices home, and later organizing. What I did not find was a clean chain from an Escuelita student to a newly founded communal institution and then evidence about how that institution’s members and children actually did over time. Zapatista influence was already traveling internationally before the Escuelita, so later resemblance alone doesn’t prove descent. I’m borrowing a pedagogy and a replication ambition, not claiming the Zapatistas already proved my whole model.

Sociocracy reaches some similar forms from a very different history: circles, consent, distributed authority, and links between levels. The resemblance doesn’t prove a universal formula. It gives builders another serious system to study instead of inventing governance during their first dispute.
